name.text: Convex Optimization - Q1: Convex Set Identification

questiontext.text:
Determine whether the following set \( S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 \) is convex:

\[ S = \{ (x, y) \mid x^2 + y^2 \le {@R2@} \} \]

The set is: [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

A set \( S \) is convex if for any two points \( \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2 \in S \), the line segment connecting them is also in \( S \). That is, \( \lambda \mathbf{x}_1 + (1-\lambda) \mathbf{x}_2 \in S \) for all \( \lambda \in [0, 1] \).

For the set \( x^2 + y^2 \le {@R2@} \), this represents a disk with radius \( {@R@} \). Since a disk is a standard example of a convex set, the answer is Convex.

Formally, the function \( f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 \) is a convex function, and the set \( \{ (x, y) \mid f(x, y) \le c \} \) is a sub-level set of a convex function, which is always convex.

questiontext.text:
Determine whether the following function \( f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) is convex:

\[ f(x) = {@a@}x^2 + {@b@}x + {@c@} \]

The function is: [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

To determine if a twice-differentiable function of one variable is convex, we check its second derivative \( f''(x) \).

1. First derivative: \( f'(x) = 2({@a@})x + {@b@} \)

2. Second derivative: \( f''(x) = 2({@a@}) = {@2*a@} \)

If \( f''(x) \ge 0 \) for all \( x \), the function is convex. Since \( {@2*a@} {@if a > 0 then ">" else "<"@} 0 \), the function is {@if a > 0 then "Convex" else "Concave (Not Convex)"@}.

questiontext.text:
Consider the feasible region defined by the following inequalities:

\[ x + y \le {@K@} \]

\[ x \ge 0, \quad y \ge 0 \]

Identify all the extreme points (vertices) of this region. Enter your answer as a set of points, e.g., {[0,0], [1,0], [0,1]}.

Extreme Points = [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

The region is a triangle in the first quadrant bounded by the axes and the line \( x + y = {@K@} \).

The extreme points occur at the intersections of the boundary lines:

  1. Intersection of \( x=0 \) and \( y=0 \): (0, 0)
  2. Intersection of \( x+y={@K@} \) and \( y=0 \): ({@K@}, 0)
  3. Intersection of \( x+y={@K@} \) and \( x=0 \): (0, {@K@})

The set of extreme points is \( \{ [0, 0], [{@K@}, 0], [0, {@K@}] \} \).

name.text: Convex Optimization - Q4: Convex Combination Property

questiontext.text:
Let \( C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \) be a nonempty set. A fundamental property states that \( C \) is convex if and only if for every finite collection of points \( \mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_k \in C \) and scalars \( \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k \ge 0 \) satisfying \( \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i = 1 \), the point \( \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i \mathbf{x}_i \in C \).

This point \( \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i \mathbf{x}_i \) is known as a:

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

The definition of a convex combination of points is \( \sum \lambda_i \mathbf{x}_i \) where \( \lambda_i \ge 0 \) and \( \sum \lambda_i = 1 \).

The property stated is a generalization of the convexity definition from two points to \( k \) points, often proved using induction. It is significant in optimization because it ensures that any point within the "span" of a set of feasible solutions is also feasible.

name.text: Convex Optimization - Q5: Feasible Region Convexity

questiontext.text:
The feasible region of a linear programming problem defined by \( \mathbf{Ax} \le \mathbf{b} \) is always a convex set. What is the geometric name for such a set (an intersection of finitely many half-spaces)?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

A set formed by the intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces is called a polyhedron (or a polytope if it is bounded).

Convexity is fundamental to optimization because in a convex problem, any local optimum is also a global optimum. The simplex method specifically exploits the fact that the optimal solution of a linear program lies at an extreme point (vertex) of this convex polyhedron.
